subject: Post-call: TTFT probe & pilot plan for Artemis Labs streaming requirements
messages:
From: Sean Gallagher <sean@redwood.com>

Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Priya Natarajan <priya@redwood.com>, Evelyn Hart <evelyn@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-05-05T14:22:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call recap and proposed TTFT probe plan

Hi Ava — thanks for taking the time today. Quick recap from our discovery on streaming / TTFT objectives and the next steps we discussed: 

Highlights from the call:
- Target TTFT: median ~150ms, 95th ~300ms, 99th under 450ms. You said sub-200ms median is ideal on mobile.
- Preferred streaming transport: WebSocket for mobile app flows, SSE for server-to-server in batch contexts. You mentioned wanting to keep both options open.
- Chunk cadence: your product team prefers initial chunk within 250–300ms for perceived responsiveness, with subsequent chunks every 100–200ms when output is long.
- Concurrency/throughput: steady-state ~120 concurrent inference sessions, bursts up to ~500 concurrent (short lived during peak).
- Session behavior: need to understand how KV cache and session affinity behave under sticky vs. stateless routing.

Proposed immediate steps (attached):
1) Run a TTFT probe using a 10k-sample workload (you mentioned you can share representative payloads).
2) Pilot config: two model variants (accuracy and quantized/low-cost) + 1 baseline routing policy to validate fallbacks.
3) Measure: median/95/99 TTFT, first-chunk latency, chunk inter-arrival, and end-to-end user-perceived time.
4) Demo: short technical deep-dive where Ben walks through runtime instrumentation and we schedule traffic-replay for next week.

Attachments: redwood-ttft-probe-plan.pdf (outline + measurement matrix)

Can you confirm the sample workload drop (or share the file) and which timezone the team prefers for an hour-long deep dive? We can run an initial synthetic probe before the demo to validate assumptions.

Thanks,

Subject: Re: Post-call recap and proposed TTFT probe plan

Thanks Sean — good summary. A few clarifications from our side: 

- WebSocket preference: correct — our mobile clients need bidirectional control messages and early partial payloads. If SSE gives better server reliability for large fan-outs we might still use it for server-only endpoints.
- TTFT tolerance: we can relax median to 200ms for initial pilot, but 95th should be under 400ms for release candidate. 99th is a soft target depending on payload length.
- Chunk cadence: initial chunk < 300ms is a hard UX ask. Subsequent chunks ideally between 80–200ms depending on server throughput.
- Concurrency: our late-night batch jobs will occasionally spike to 800 short-lived sessions (5–15s each). We want to see graceful degradation on tail latencies rather than hard failures.
- KV cache / session affinity: our infra team is specifically asking how Redwood handles cache warming when traffic is replayed across many source IPs — whether sticky routing or a shared KV warmup is required.

I've attached a sanitized sample of our recent request traces and a 5k sample payloads file: artemis-sample-workload.jsonl. Please let us know if you need additional fields.

We can do the technical deep-dive next Tue May 11 at 10:00 PT or Wed May 12 at 14:00 PT. Which works best for your infra folks?

Regards,

Hi Ava — Ben from Solutions Engineering here. Quick technical notes and a proposed pilot/runbook attached. Summarizing how Redwood will approach the probes and what we'll measure: 

1) Transport & session affinity
- Both WebSocket and SSE are first-class. WebSocket keeps a long-lived connection which lets us maintain a per-connection KV cache and reduce cold starts; SSE is stateless per-request by default but can be paired with sticky routing for affinity.
- For traffic-replay we recommend enabling a routing key that maps to a digest of the session id so replayed traffic will hit the same cache warmups when possible. If replay from many IPs is unavoidable, we will run a warmup stage to pre-populate common kv prefixes.

2) Pilot configuration (proposal)
- Step 0: dry run synthetic probe (no auth, synthetic traces) to validate measurement pipeline.
- Step 1: traffic replay using your artemis-sample-workload.jsonl at baseline concurrency (120), measure TTFT median/95/99 and chunk timings.
- Step 2: controlled burst tests up to 800 concurrent short sessions to observe tail behavior and fallback thresholds.
- Step 3: model variant comparison: default vs 4-bit quantized. Note: quantized variant expected to reduce cost and TTFT slightly but we'll validate.

3) Chunk cadence recommendations
- Target first chunk: < 250–300ms (optimize prompt priming and small-token-first emissions).
- Subsequent chunks: 80–200ms depending on average token rate; for mobile clients we recommend 100–150ms to balance perceived smoothness and network power.
- If the model produces many short tokens, we will enable chunk aggregation to avoid too many tiny frames.

4) Metrics and instrumentation we will provide
- Per-request TTFT, first-chunk time, subsequent chunk inter-arrival, model compute time, queuing time, kcache hit rate, and host-level GPU utilization.
- We will also provide a sampling of request/response traces for failed/slow tails.

Attached: pilot-runbook.md (step-by-step) and a short test plan. I'm happy to walk through this during the deep-dive.
